title: Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
content:
Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on GoogleThe Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.
The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.
The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.
The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.
France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.
The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.
Goals downgraded
The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.
Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.
But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”
Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.
“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.
A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

title: Haute-Savoie: de nouvelles aides débloquées pour éviter la fuite des soignants vers la Suisse
content:
Haute-Savoie: de nouvelles aides débloquées pour éviter la fuite des soignants vers la Suisse
Des aides financières d'ampleur pour faire face à la fuite des soignants vers la Suisse (et ses salaires). Au début du mois de septembre, la Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie (CPAM) et l'Agence de santé (ARS) d'Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes ont annoncé de nouvelles mesures pour favoriser l'implantation des infirmiers libéraux en Haute-Savoie et dans l'Ain.
Une aide de 45.000 euros est par exemple proposée aux premières installations dans quatre secteurs définis: les environs de Saint-Julien-en-Genevois, Annemasse et La Roche-sur-Foron pour la Haute-Savoie, et Gex pour l’Ain.
Pointant les deux départements "directement concernés par la proximité avec la Suisse", où la rémunération est plus avantageuse, l'ARS justifie ces révisions dans un communiqué publié le 9 septembre: "la situation en matière de densité d’infirmiers libéraux est particulièrement difficile, alors même que les besoins de soins de la population sont importants".
Aides au maintien et à l'installation
En plus de l'aide à la première installation, des contrats incitatifs sont aussi proposés pour le maintien ou la simple installation. Concernant les infirmiers déjà installés, ceux qui se maintiennent dans les zones en tension pourront bénéficier d'un coup de pouce de 3.600 euros par an.
Ces mesures, entrées en vigueur à compter du 1er septembre, portent un objectif double selon l'ARS: "faciliter l’arrivée de nouveaux professionnels et encourager les infirmiers déjà installés à poursuivre leur activité dans ces territoires".
La réforme apparaît en effet comme un impératif dans les territoires concernés: "Il y a eu une augmentation de l'attractivité de la Suisse. Les personnels paramédicaux qui travaillent en Suisse ont augmenté de 60% en dix ans. On avait donc besoin d'une solution pour inciter les infirmiers à travailler côté français", développe pour France 3 Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Romain Henry, directeur adjoint de la CPAM de Haute-Savoie.

title: Menschliche Originalität: Wie kreativ macht uns KI wirklich?
content:
Menschliche Originalität : Wie kreativ macht uns KI wirklich?
Künstliche Intelligenz hilft Menschen beim Schreiben von Büchern, Musik und Studien. Aber auch in überraschenden Bereichen hilft sie den Menschen über so manche Hemmschwelle hinweg.
Welchen Wert hat die Kunst? Interessanterweise war das für Ökonomen lange Zeit eher ein nebensächliches Thema. Dabei sind Künstler – mögen es Schriftsteller, Bildhauer oder auch Theaterleute sein – im besten Fall Menschen mit innovativen und originellen Ideen. Darin unterscheiden sie sich gar nicht so sehr von einer Berufsgruppe, die Ökonomen stets brennend interessiert hat: den Unternehmern.
Nun haben die Künstler durchaus auch selbst dazu beigetragen, dass sich die Wirtschaftswelt eher wenig mit ihnen beschäftigt hat. In einem lesenswerten Aufsatz zum Wesen der Kreativität hat der Forscher David Galenson vor einigen Jahren festgestellt, dass Künstler schon immer darum bemüht waren, sich abzugrenzen. Exemplarisch dafür steht ein berühmter Ausspruch Vincent van Goghs, der 1884 an einen befreundeten Maler schrieb: „Die Kunst ist – obwohl sie von menschlichen Händen erstellt wird – nie nur ein Resultat dieser Hände allein, sondern stammt von einer tieferen Quelle in unseren Seelen.“
Diese tiefere Quelle kann seinem Verständnis nach Gott sein, was die Kunst in den Augen vieler Künstler schon immer zu etwas Übernatürlichem, zutiefst Besonderem gemacht hat. Vielleicht erklärt gerade das den Schock, den die Erfindung des Sprachroboters ChatGPT bei vielen kreativen Menschen ausgelöst hat: Plötzlich kann jeder kreativ sein. Nötig ist dafür allein das Formulieren eines einfachen „Prompts“, wie die Anweisungen heißen, die die Nutzer der Künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) geben.
Das mag manch ein Künstler als Beleidigung empfinden. Für den Durchschnittsmenschen ist es aber erfreulich. Der Industrieländer-Club OECD wertet regelmäßig die Auswirkungen Künstlicher Intelligenz auf verschiedene Felder wie Produktivität, Innovation und Kreativität aus. Im Jahr 2025 hat die Organisation festgestellt, was man schon aus anderen Bereichen kennt: Die KI kann unerfahrene Schreiber besser machen. In einem Experiment zum Verfassen von Kurzgeschichten wirkten diese Geschichten auf die Leser neuartiger und origineller, wenn KI dabei zum Einsatz kam. Vergleicht man allerdings eine Vielzahl von Kurzgeschichten miteinander, die auf diese Weise entstanden sind, so zeigt sich: Mochte die einzelne Geschichte origineller wirken, so war die Bandbreite dieser Originalität dann doch begrenzt. Sprich: Die Muster ähnelten einander, was kein Wunder ist. Schließlich bedienten sich ja alle des gleichen Rohmaterials, der Daten von ChatGPT.
Nun macht die KI beständig Fortschritte, das Manko ist heutzutage also womöglich nicht mehr so groß. Ein Experiment mit 600 Teilnehmern zeigt aber, wo mögliche Schwachstellen liegen. Noch scheint es so zu sein, dass erfahrene Schreiber eher an Originalität einbüßen, wenn sie in ihren Texten zu Teilen auf Künstliche Intelligenz vertrauen. Die Untersuchung eines Forscherteams der Universität Exeter aus dem Jahr 2024, in KI-Zeiten also vor einer halben Ewigkeit, stellte fest: Wer bereits vor dem Schreiben des ersten Satzes auf KI setzte, begrenzte sich durch diese Vorauswahl in der Art und Weise, wie er den Text formulieren würde.
Plakativ lässt sich das anhand eines Beispiels zeigen, das der amerikanische Neurowissenschaftler Adam Green so formuliert: „Menschen können aufgrund ihrer persönlichen Erfahrungen ungewöhnliche Assoziationen haben. So kann es sein, dass jemand eine Wassermelone mit Fußball assoziiert. Solche Assoziationen können bei jedem Menschen unterschiedlich sein.“ Diese Unterschiedlichkeit könne KI nur schwer abbilden, was ihre kreativen Fähigkeiten begrenze. Greens ganz praktischer Tipp lautet darum: immer zunächst mit eigenen Ideen beginnen und erst dann die KI hinzuziehen.
Bevor es aber nun zu negativ wird, sei auf andere erstaunliche Fortschritte verwiesen, in denen die KI Menschen tatsächlich kreativer und produktiver macht: Der Ausstoß wissenschaftlicher Studien zählt dazu. Er ist deutlich gestiegen. Das ließe sich leicht als Zeichen des Verfalls wissenschaftlicher Arbeitsweisen interpretieren, in denen man der KI die Schreibarbeit überlässt und ihren Einsatz zu vertuschen sucht. Doch Forscher haben eine andere Erklärung: Tatsächlich konnten vor allem jene Akademiker die Zahl ihrer Schriften steigern, die keine englischen Muttersprachler sind. Da Englisch aber die weltweit wichtigste Wissenschaftssprache ist, verschafft der Einsatz kluger Übersetzungsprogramme dem Rest der Welt etwas mehr Chancengleichheit.
In den Vereinigten Staaten wiederum gibt es eine interessante Art der Selbstermächtigung, die ebenfalls aus dem Aufkommen der KI resultiert: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Menschen, die ohne Hilfe eines Rechtsanwalts eine Klage einreichen, seit 2022 in etwa verdoppelt. Die Vermutung ist: Die KI hat beim Verfassen der Klage geholfen. Über die Erfolgsaussichten sagt dies allerdings noch nichts aus.
Eines fällt übrigens in fast allen kreativen Bereichen auf – egal, ob es nun um Texte oder gar um KI-generierte Musik geht: So gerne die Menschen selbst KI einsetzen, so wenig mögen sie es, wenn ihnen Musik oder Texte präsentiert werden, die allein durch Künstliche Intelligenz entstanden sind. Menschliche Originalität, so könnte man daraus schließen, hat noch immer einen Wert.

title: Aluno de Almada já tem escola, após condenação do Ministério
content:
O aluno do concelho de Almada com necessidades educativas especiais, que o Ministério da Educação foi condenado a colocar numa escola daquele município, “já se encontra colocado na Escola Básica das Lagoas”, informou a Agência para a Gestão do Sistema Educativo (AGSE).
Segundo a AGSE, “o aluno em questão já se encontra colocado na Escola Básica das Lagoas, tendo sido igualmente mobilizados os recursos humanos necessários para assegurar o respetivo acompanhamento e apoio educativo”.
“O Tribunal Administrativo e Fiscal de Almada foi, entretanto, informado das diligências realizadas”, acrescentou.
Na sexta-feira, o Movimento para a Inclusão Efetiva anunciara que o Ministério da Educação fora condenado a colocar uma criança com necessidades educativas especiais numa escola do concelho de Almada, onde reside, com os apoios pedagógicos de que necessita.
O coordenador do movimento, Lourenço Santos, disse à Lusa que a decisão do Tribunal Administrativo e Fiscal de Almada, conhecida na sexta-feira, decorreu de uma ação interposta pelos pais da criança, que pretendiam que o filho fosse colocado numa escola da sua área de residência com os devidos recursos pedagógicos.
Segundo Lourenço Santos, o tribunal deu três dias úteis para o Ministério da Educação colocar a criança numa escola do concelho onde reside, devendo-lhe ser assegurados “100 por cento dos recursos necessários” e identificados no relatório técnico-pedagógico, documento que fundamenta e define medidas de suporte à aprendizagem e à inclusão de um aluno, tais como um professor especializado.

title: Florida restringirá uso de inteligencia artificial en escuelas y universidades desde 2027
content:
Florida impondrá nuevas restricciones al uso de la inteligencia artificial (IA) en escuelas y universidades públicas, sumándose a las medidas adoptadas por los distritos escolares de Los Ángeles y Nueva York ante las crecientes preocupaciones sobre el impacto de esta tecnología en la educación.
El Consejo de Educación de Florida aprobó por unanimidad nuevas limitaciones a la IA en escuelas públicas de preescolar a secundaria y en las universidades públicas estatales, incluyendo prohibir esta tecnología para “satisfacer las necesidades sociales” de los alumnos o “simular amistad, compañía o relaciones emocionales” con ellos.
La normativa también impedirá que los alumnos empleen inteligencia artificial para realizar trabajos o evaluaciones calificadas de un curso o programa. Asimismo, restringirá el uso de sistemas con diseños antropomórficos o destinados a establecer relaciones que incentiven a los estudiantes a continuar interactuando con la herramienta.
- LEA TAMBIÉN: Los líderes de la IA piden reducir su desarrollo, pero la competencia dificulta el acuerdo
Las medidas, que afectarán a más de 3 millones de estudiantes a partir de julio de 2027, también obligan a las escuelas a obtener consentimiento de los padres sobre la implementación de estas herramientas y, si las rechazan, los planteles deberán proporcionar alternativas de enseñanza sin inteligencia artificial.
La alarma nacional por la IA
Las medidas de Florida contra la IA se aprueban semanas después de restricciones avaladas por los distritos escolares de Los Ángeles y Nueva York, los dos mayores de Estados Unidos, seguidos por el de Miami.
Mientras Los Ángeles anunció la prohibición de la IA generativa de texto, imágenes y otro contenido, Nueva York emitió una moratoria de un año de esta tecnología para niños desde preescolar hasta octavo grado.
Casi la mitad de los estados en EE.UU., 24, han emitido lineamientos para la IA en las aulas, según la organización civil TeachAI, mientras la asociación FutureEd ha documentado 77 proyectos de ley en 27 estados que abordan la inteligencia artificial en la enseñanza.
En contraste, el gobernador de Florida, el republicano Ron DeSantis, advirtió el lunes a los miembros de su partido que apoyar la IA será una “posición perdedora” en las próximas elecciones.
Con información de EFE.

title: Coastal cleanup campaign held in Bilgah at Leyla Aliyeva's initiative
content:
Coastal cleanup campaign held in Bilgah at Leyla Aliyeva's initiative
- 22 September, 2026
- 13:39
A coastal cleanup campaign was organized at a public beach in Bilgah settlement at the initiative of Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of IDEA Public Union, Report informs.
Over 150 volunteers participated in IDEA's "Keep the coasts clean!" campaign to mark World Cleanup Day and the end of the beach season. All waste, amounting to more than 2 tons, collected by the participants of the action, which were equipped with the necessary sanitary equipment during the cleaning were delivered to the Balakhani solid household waste sorting plant of "Tamiz Sheher" OJSC.
The main objective of the initiative is to promote compliance with cleanliness on the sea coasts, prevent pollution of coastal areas with household waste and attract people to efforts to protect the marine environment.
To protect the unique biodiversity of the Caspian Sea and other water bodies of the Caucasus region, IDEA organizes regular measures aimed at cleaning and restoring polluted coastal areas.
The Public Union continues to call on citizens to support nature conservation efforts and keep shorelines clean, helping build a healthier, cleaner, and more sustainable future for generations to come.

title: ONG alertan que miles de venezolanos se enfrentan a consecuencias a largo plazo tras los terremotos
content:
Las ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español han alertado de que, a medida que la respuesta a los terremotos que azotaron el centro y norte de Venezuela avanza hacia una fase de recuperación temprana, "miles de personas se enfrentan a las consecuencias a largo plazo del desastre, agravadas por las fuertes lluvias y el inicio del retorno a las aulas".
La organización se activó el pasado 25 de junio para responder a esta grave emergencia, con la participación de ocho ONG --Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision-- que "continúan trabajando de manera multisectorial en las regiones más afectadas, incluyendo el Distrito Capital, La Guaira, Miranda y Falcón, con planes de expansión hacia Carabobo y Aragua".
El Comité de Emergencia Español señaló que "la protección infantil, la continuidad educativa, la salud mental y la atención primaria de salud, vivienda, agua, saneamiento e higiene y asistencia alimentaria" constituyen "las prioridades absolutas en este momento" de la emergencia.
La organización destacó que el regreso a la actividad escolar ilustra la complejidad de la situación actual, ya que "la comunidad educativa requiere urgentemente de protocolos claros de actuación, rutas de evacuación y espacios preparados que eviten la toma de decisiones improvisadas ante posibles réplicas y que, al mismo tiempo, contengan las secuelas emocionales y el duelo de los estudiantes".
El Comité precisó que "para garantizar la dignidad, la autonomía y la capacidad de resiliencia de la población en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad, los esfuerzos de las 8 ONG internacionales especialistas en ayuda humanitaria" se articulan en torno a necesidades estructurales específicas de protección y acompañamiento psicosocial.
En materia de agua y saneamiento, la organización indicó que "tras haberse distribuido millones de litros de agua potable, las acciones se centran en el mantenimiento de infraestructuras esenciales en barrios y residencias de mayores, incluyendo la instalación de tanques, grifos y duchas inclusivas, así como el suministro de miles de kits de higiene familiar".
El Comité explicó que los programas educativos "permiten el reparto de kits de materiales, la reconstrucción de infraestructuras escolares dañadas y el diseño de modalidades híbridas o semipresenciales para facilitar el retorno seguro de más de 26.500 estudiantes, junto con la creación de espacios temporales de aprendizaje".
La organización señaló que en materia de asistencia sanitaria "se desarrollan jornadas móviles de atención médica y nutrición, soporte especializado para madres y bebés, y entrega de ayuda de primera necesidad, como alimentos y medicamentos", además de acompañamiento para restablecer medios de subsistencia.
La directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira, subrayó que "la reconstrucción trasciende a la entrega de ayuda material inmediata" y "exige un compromiso sostenido en el tiempo que dote a la ciudadanía y líderes comunitarios de las herramientas logísticas y emocionales necesarias para organizar la respuesta de sus propias comunidades".
Barbeira concluyó que "las necesidades sobre el terreno continúan en Venezuela" y ha apelado a mantener el apoyo, afirmando que "para que las familias en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad reconstruyan sus vidas y recuperen su independencia, el apoyo sostenido es indispensable".

title: Scientists identify first new wild cat species in more than a century
content:
Named Leopardus tilcayo, the small spotted cat lives in the Yungas cloud forests on the eastern slopes of the Andes. It is smaller than an average domestic cat, measuring about 18 inches from head to the end of its body and weighing roughly 1.36 kg (3 pounds).
The discovery began in 2016, when Bolivian biologist and National Geographic Explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz was called to the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after a local man brought in what he believed was a domestic kitten.
The animal had been found on a road near a forest and raised for about a year. Its owner eventually realized that it was wild and could not care for it.

Nogales-Ascarrunz initially believed the cat belonged to Leopardus tigrinus, a species commonly known as the tiger cat, oncilla or little spotted cat.
But in 2019, while preparing a guide to Bolivia’s wild cats, she noticed that the animal’s large rosettes did not match those of tiger cats shown in reference material from neighboring Brazil.
Further genetic research eventually confirmed that the animal belonged to a distinct lineage. Researchers analyzed genetic material from the sanctuary cat and another individual that later arrived at Senda Verde. The two animals were found to belong to the same species, which diverged from other tiger cat lineages about 1.4 million years ago. The findings were published Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
The scientific name Leopardus tilcayo comes from the name used by local communities for the animal. Nogales-Ascarrunz said people in the area have known the cat as a “tilcayo” for generations, although they do not associate the word with a particular meaning in Spanish or local Indigenous languages. The researchers chose to preserve the traditional name rather than give the species a new one.
The discovery also changes scientists’ understanding of tiger cats. The new study identifies five distinct tiger cat species in South America, showing that what was once considered a single species was actually a complex of genetically distinct lineages.
Small wild cats are difficult to study because they are elusive and often inhabit remote forests. Physical characteristics such as coat patterns, tail length and teeth can help distinguish species, but the researchers used genomic analysis to establish the tilcayo’s distinct position on the cat family tree.

The team analyzed the genomes of 38 cats, including 26 Leopardus specimens. Unlike some recently recognized mammals that were split from already known species, L. tilcayo had not previously been identified by scientists. Researchers found no museum specimens that had been collected and identified as the species.
Its population in the wild remains unknown.
Nogales-Ascarrunz is now working to install camera traps in the Yungas forests to find more evidence of the species and determine how many tilcayos remain.
The researchers say the discovery also highlights the need to protect the Yungas, where development and agriculture are putting pressure on habitats used by tiger cats and other wildlife.

title: A fuoco l’Oasi Lipu Soglitelle a Villa Literno
content:
L’Oasi Lipu, in Campania, è stata colpita da un incendio a pochi giorni dal riconoscimento europeo dell’area con l’istituzione della Zona di protezione speciale (Zps). Il Coordinatore delle Guardie Lipu Paolella: “è bruciato un miracolo”
L’Oasi Lipu Soglitelle, nel territorio di Villa Literno, in Campania, è stato colpito da un incendio. Secondo quanto riferito dalla Lipu, le fiamme avrebbero interessato soltanto la strada di accesso all’area protetta, provocando però gravi danni al ponte, che era stato recentemente riparato. L’episodio arriva a pochi giorni dal riconoscimento europeo dell’area con l’istituzione della Zps, Zona di protezione speciale, nell’ambito della rete Natura 2000 e delle direttive europee Uccelli e Habitat.
L’oasi rappresenta uno dei simboli della trasformazione di un territorio segnato in passato da criminalità e degrado. La zona, ricorda la Lipu, era stata utilizzata per lo scarico illegale di rifiuti e per attività di bracconaggio ai danni degli uccelli migratori. Attraverso l’operazione “Volo Libero”, condotta insieme ai carabinieri forestali, l’area è stata progressivamente sottratta a queste pratiche e trasformata in una riserva naturale e in uno spazio dedicato alla tutela ambientale, all’educazione e alla fruizione pubblica.
Maurizio Paolella, Coordinatore Guardie Lipu Caserta ha scritto un lungo posto sui social in cui ha commentato: “Non è bruciata una sterpaglia. È bruciato un miracolo. Un pezzo di terra martoriata dalla camorra, dai veleni, dagli sversamenti, che finalmente stava tornando a vivere. Che era diventata ZPS – Zona di Protezione Speciale. Che era diventata Casa per centinaia di uccelli, per la natura, per i nostri figli. E guarda caso brucia PROPRIO ORA. Proprio dopo che è stata istituita la ZPS. Proprio dopo che quell’area ha iniziato ad avere regole, tutele, occhi addosso. (…) anno bruciato canneti, nidi, vite. Hanno bruciato il lavoro di volontari che da anni, gratis, sotto il sole, cercavano di restituirci un pezzo di paradiso rubato”.

title: GREEN LUNG BOOST: Turning the corner — steady revival of Nelson Mandela Bay’s oldest park
content:
The oldest public park in the Bay has seen better days, garnering a reputation for harbouring vagrants and criminals seeking to prey on unsuspecting visitors.
Much of the park’s assets and infrastructure, such as a public pool and various sports facilities, have fallen into disrepair due to theft, vandalism and neglect, adding to the stigma surrounding the once-beautiful public space.
However, over the past three years, thanks to some much-needed attention from volunteers and local businesses in the community, alongside strategic partnerships between private entities and public directorates, St George’s Park has slowly started to turn the corner.
The municipality has spent a tidy sum on security upgrades around the park, while interest groups like the Friends of St George’s Park have launched initiatives to get more feet through the gates. Now the ruling government coalition’s biggest political rival, the DA, is drawing up plans to turn it into “Gqeberha’s Central Park”.
Whether it be nostalgia, a sense of community, or a need to provide the city with a safe public space, it seems St George’s Park has managed to transcend political divides, and everyone wants to see the park restored to its former glory.
“We appreciate any attention the park gets, but we want to move away from the polarising nature of politics and we certainly don’t want the park to become a political tool. The park is more important than that, and we want it to become a space where everyone can come together,” said André Theron of the Friends of St George’s Park.
R100m revamp pledge
This comes after Democratic Alliance mayoral candidate Retief Odendaal and several senior party members pledged R100-million towards revamping the park and its facilities, should the party win the upcoming local government elections. They conducted an oversight visit to St George’s Park last week.
While the group looked at several decaying facilities, and wanted to lay the blame at the feet of the city’s current leadership, a conversation with Odendaal afterwards specifically focused on bringing communities together.
“The park is situated in one of the most densely populated regions of Nelson Mandela Bay, and we have a diverse mix of scholars, students, professionals and families that live around it. Regardless of their political affiliations, these people need a safe space to go outside, go for a walk, to kick a ball.
Gqeberha’s Central Park?
“St George’s Park can be that. It has the potential to become for Gqeberha what Central Park is to New York,” said Odendaal.
The park was first opened in 1861. At the time it was surrounded by the manor homes of the city’s wealthiest and most influential families.
It is home to Pearson Conservatory, imported from the UK and erected in 1882, while St George’s Park, the oldest cricket grounds on South African soil, opened its pitch in 1889.
Over the years, and with the development of the Central neighbourhood as Gqeberha’s business hub, several apartment blocks were constructed and the area around the park became more densely populated.
Recreational facilities had to be developed along with the surrounding area, and over time the park became home to lawn bowls clubs, tennis clubs, the Mannville open air theatre, the Prince Alfred’s Guard Memorial, a borehole project to supplement the city’s water supply, as well as play parks and expansive public gardens.
State of decline
Sadly, as Central steadily declined, the park became unsafe and a hive of criminal activity, in turn leading to the deterioration of its many assets.
A prime example is the St George’s public swimming pool.
First opened in 1937, the 150-foot (45m) pool hosted many swimming galas while the main stands were packed with spectators. It was also a popular destination for bathers who preferred the pool to the beach during the summer season.
That is hard to believe when looking at the current state of the pool complex.
Deep trenches run along the sides of the pool where thieves dug up the piping, while the diving boards are inaccessible after the metal stairs were also stripped. In the ablution blocks and dressing rooms, basins and urinals have been destroyed, weeds grow out of toilet bowls and walls are scorched where vagrants lit fires.
According to the DA’s spokesperson for Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture in Nelson Mandela Bay, Sebezile Rafani, the city has budgeted a paltry R900,000 towards the pool. However, there is no clear indication what the funds are for, and the money has never been spent.
Municipal spokesperson Sithembiso Soyaya said the city acknowledges the state of the pool and that steps are being taken towards its restoration.
“The municipality is in the process of acquiring the services of a suitably qualified service provider to conduct a professional assessment of the work required, including the associated costs. There are also challenges relating to underground water, which have an impact on the repair or possible reconstruction of the pool itself.”
With regards to the broader park issues, Soyaya said improved security and access control was a major step towards the St George’s revival.
“The fencing around the park was redone, which improved access control and strengthened security within the facility. This was followed by the deployment of security officers to patrol the area.”
Soyaya said the Parks and Cemeteries sub-directorate also conducts monthly grass cutting and general maintenance operations throughout the park.
While he did not disclose the cost of the fencing upgrade, Theron said this was one of the initiatives the Friends of St George’s Park appreciated a lot as it came at a “hefty cost”.
“Security remains the biggest priority, and the new fence and gates is a major boon for the park.
“Our teams have partnered with a local homeless shelter MES, and are working closely with city officials. We conduct regular clean-ups of gardens and flower beds. Besides beautification, this also removes possible hiding spots for criminals and their loot, further improving security.”
He said the next step would hopefully include CCTV systems and additional lighting throughout the park.
Over the three years since the Friends of St George’s Park was established, Theron said their biggest goal was to get more people into the park, which in turn played a role in driving out vagrants and criminal elements.
The friends established a well-supported weekly Park Run, and hosted several Silent Book Club events, while an art exhibition in collaboration with painter Wessel Kotzee in December 2025 brought upwards of 1,500 people to the Pearson Conservatory.
“The Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality appreciates the efforts of the Friends of St George’s Park and their cooperative relationship with the Municipality’s Parks and Cemeteries sub-directorate in contributing to the upkeep of the park,” Soyaya said.
“Public participation and partnerships with community organisations remain important in complementing the municipality’s efforts to maintain public facilities and open spaces,” he added. DM

title: Welsh communities given support to build local energy projects to tackle climate change
content:
Welsh communities given support to build local energy projects to tackle climate change
Communities across Wales will receive a funding boost to build and control their own clean energy supply
- Great British Energy rolls out first wave of biggest public community energy investment in UK history, backing local places to cut bills and take climate action.
- Community energy groups can access more funding to build their own clean power projects.
- Communities to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects, ensuring proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas.
Communities across Wales will receive a funding boost to build and control their own clean energy supply that will help to cut bills, grow local wealth and tackle the climate crisis – with the rollout of the biggest UK public investment in community energy.
Great British Energy is today (17 September) launching £30 million funding to kick start a community power revolution – the first downpayment on up to £1 billion, announced earlier this year - with the aim to support over 1000 local and community-led clean energy projects across the UK.
Building on Wales’ existing commitment to community energy through the Welsh Government Energy Service, the new funding will enable more community energy groups to accelerate plans for locally owned clean power projects - from solar panels on local buildings to village-owned wind farms and hydro schemes in nearby rivers. This will help to put money back in the pockets of communities and allow them join in UK-wide climate action, following the record temperatures reached this summer due to climate change.
These will be owned by community energy groups, meaning local areas can reap the full benefits – from reduced bills for local services to ensuring profits from the clean power generated flow back into towns and villages, rather than just to energy companies.
After the heatwaves and extreme weather events seen this year, this funding will expand communities’ opportunities to helping tackle climate change, building on the support provided by Welsh Government and its delivery partners - empowering them to move away from fossil fuels with their own clean energy supply that will help cut emissions and protect their local area.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:
All of us felt deep concern for our climate during the record-breaking temperatures we experienced this summer.
Ahead of New York Climate week, we are putting power in the hands of people and places, so more communities can take action.
Everyone deserves a stake in our energy future and through these local power projects, communities can reap the full benefits of clean energy – reducing emissions, cutting bills and reinvesting profits to benefit local areas, instead of big energy companies.
Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said:
Communities across Wales will be able to build more of their own clean energy projects with grants from the UK Government.
This project puts decision-making into the hands of local people, giving them the power to bring down household bills and be part of our national effort to tackle climate change.
CEO of Great British Energy Dan McGrail said:
Great British Energy is continuing to put communities at the heart of the clean energy transition with the GBE Community Fund and Partnerships Grant. Our vision is that every community should have the chance to build and own its own renewable energy. These grants will give community organisations and local authorities the practical support they need to get clean energy projects off the ground - lowering bills, supporting jobs and putting the benefits from energy into local hands.
Alongside funding specific local power projects, the government will also set out further details this Autumn on plans for community energy groups to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects.
This aims to create partnerships between communities and developers that will see proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas. It will bring Britain in line with countries like Germany and Denmark, where this type of ownership set up is already widely used – allowing communities to benefit directly from local clean power.
Several such partnerships are already being developed in Wales and the work by GBE could help widen access to more communities.
Notes to Editors
-
Local ownership is already breathing new life into neighbourhoods across the country, reviving pubs, libraries and leisure centres. But for too long, community-run energy projects have been held back by a lack of funding, advice and government support.
-
Great British Energy is working with the Welsh Government to change this, as applications have opened today for new grants to support community energy projects Wales.in the first wave of up to £1 billion in support to put clean energy back in the hand of communities.
-
This builds on £9.5 million Great British Energy and the Welsh Government have already allocated to install solar panels on public buildings across Wales, such as schools, leisure centres and museums across, under the Welsh Government’s Wales Funding Programme. The funding has also backed the Welsh Government’s new Ymestyn scheme, which will help communities and the Welsh public sector to complete projects such as solar canopies and battery energy storage, to help cut energy bills and lower emissions. The Great British Energy support launched in Wales today includes:
-
The £20 million Community Fund - offers grant funding to help community organisations across England, Wales and Northern Ireland to test, develop and build community-owned clean energy assets. Projects supported by this fund must demonstrate that the community will hold a defined legal and financial interest in the project, and that a defined share of project benefits will be retained for, or delivered to, the local community.
-
Advice services – Great British Energy is also backing organisations that offer crucial advice to local groups on the development of community energy initiatives with £2.8 million support for advice services across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
-
Great British Energy is also seeking information from investors to help size and scope its future products.

title: SBS aprueba reglamento para gestionar riesgo de sobreendeudamiento cooperativo
content:
La Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP (SBS) aprobó el Reglamento para la administración del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento de los socios deudores minoristas de las cooperativas de ahorro y crédito no autorizadas a captar recursos del público (Coopac), con el objetivo de fortalecer la gestión de dicho riesgo en el sistema cooperativo.


El reglamento busca promover el crecimiento responsable y sostenible de las colocaciones, sobre la base de una adecuada evaluación de su capacidad de pago.
En ese sentido, la norma establece estándares mínimos para la administración del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento. De igual modo, se incorporan reportes diseñados como herramientas de gestión —tableros de control— para que los funcionarios y directivos de las Coopac evalúen, monitoreen y realicen el seguimiento de dicho riesgo.
Para una adecuada gestión del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento, la norma también precisa responsabilidades para el Consejo de Administración y la Gerencia General, así como funciones específicas para el Comité de Riesgos, la Unidad de Riesgos y la Unidad de Auditoría Interna.
Cabe destacar que, la SBS – en el marco de su compromiso con el fortalecimiento del sistema cooperativo – lleva varios meses desarrollando talleres teóricos y prácticos, dirigidos a los funcionarios y directivos de las Coopac, sobre la gestión del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento y la elaboración e implementación de los reportes previstos en el reglamento; los cuales se tiene previsto continuar desarrollando en las próximas semanas a fin de fortalecer su desarrollo y adecuada implementación.

title: 沉浸式科普点亮青少年"爱农强农"植保梦
content: 时值九月，序属三秋，天高云淡，金风送爽。为践行人与自然和谐共生理念，厚植青少年爱农知农强农情怀，2026年9月19日，中国农业科学院植物保护研究所以"新植保赋能生态治理，全健康护航粮食安全"为主题，面向社会公众开展沉浸式科普教育，举办第八届农科开放日专场科普活动。 观测农药非靶标生物。 来自人大附中西山学校、中国农大附小、中关村第一小学等数十所学校的中小学生，在家长陪同下走进植保所院区，奔赴植保知识小课堂、科研实践微体验、趣味互动小游戏三大主题活动板块。据植保所李宁博士介绍，活动坚持科普为民，统筹知识性、趣味性、体验感，把实验室前沿科研成果转化为通俗易懂、可感可参与的科普内容，推动高端科研资源向社会科普资源转化。 观察啮齿动物头骨标本。 植保知识小课堂内，科研人员紧扣社会关注热点开展专题科普宣讲。陈景超博士以"给生态留点'鼠'空间"为题，介绍草原鼠害科学防控理念，破除"灭鼠就要赶尽杀绝"的片面认知。人大附中西山学校学生梁以沫说："通过'三分钟识别外来入侵物种'科普，我认识了加拿大一枝黄花等危险入侵生物。"活动面向青少年及家长普及农业生物安全知识，引导全社会树牢生物安全风险防范意识，夯实农业生物安全的群众基础。 动手体验豇豆农药残留快速检测。 科研实践微体验区向参观者开放农作物、杂草、啮齿动物、各类昆虫标本资源。"小小农残侦探"体验点位上，同学们动手操作农残检测试纸，完整体验农产品质量安全检测流程；现场演示病毒检测试剂盒实操实验，把实验室科研场景搬到科普一线；张浩文博士依托昆虫雷达科普展台，深入浅出讲解虫情监测预警技术原理；黄红娟博士借助寄生植物列当科普展板，生动讲述农田生态中奇妙的植物攻防关系。 孩子们参加寻宝大作战活动，找寻白星花金龟幼虫。 趣味游戏互动区设置了丰富的互动项目。孩子们在闯关游戏中区分益虫与害虫，学习昆虫生物学特性、生物防治等专业知识，实现寓教于乐。一位学生家长表示，这类科普跳出课本局限，让孩子看得见、摸得着，真正读懂保障国家粮食安全、维护生态保护的时代意义。 杂草鼠害与草地有害生物防控中心主任刘晓辉研究员表示，新时代植物保护工作，要摒弃简单灭杀的传统思路，牢固树立生命共同体理念，综合运用生态调控、绿色防控技术，统筹农业生产发展与生物多样性保护，践行人与自然和谐共生的"全健康"理念，以科技创新守护粮食安全与生态安全。 植保所副所长陈捷胤表示，用好农科开放日平台，开展好科普服务，是科研"国家队"履行社会责任的重要实践，帮助青少年厚植热爱农科、敬畏自然的理想种子，为培育知农爱农时代新人积蓄力量。植保所纪委书记刘水长表示，植保所将发挥国家级科研院所科普示范作用，不断丰富科普载体、创新科普形式，面向社会大众普及植物保护、农业生物安全相关知识，助力提升全民科学素养。 活动由植保所党委办公室、杂草鼠害与草地有害生物防控中心承办，累计吸引600余个家庭、近2000名群众参与。 （本文图片均由中国农科院植保所提供）

title: Sacred springs of South Africa—pure waters or polluted? We found tiny bits of plastic in the samples we tested
content:
Across South Africa, natural springs are more than sources of freshwater. Some are places of healing, spiritual cleansing and rituals, where communities collect water and maintain longstanding cultural connections with the environment. For example, during cleansing rituals, people bathe in or collect spring water as a way of seeking spiritual renewal, healing and protection. These are known as sacred springs.
We are a team of environmental scientists and freshwater biologists interested in water quality, freshwater biodiversity and disturbances.
We set out to investigate an emerging form of pollution—microplastics—in nine sacred, unique and frequently visited freshwater springs in South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces.
We selected these springs because they are locally recognized as culturally and spiritually important, but before this study, scientists had not investigated whether they were polluted.
These sacred freshwater springs are quite remote and isolated. Still, our research found microplastics in all nine. We detected 184 particles in total, with concentrations ranging from 5 to 48 particles per liter.
There is no internationally agreed safe level of microplastics in freshwater or drinking water, so these concentrations cannot be described simply as "safe" or "unsafe." Results also vary because researchers use different methods to collect and test samples. A one-liter sample from these springs could therefore contain anywhere from just a handful to dozens of tiny plastic particles.
Although we cannot use this number alone to say whether the water is harmful to people, it shows that microplastic pollution is present and gives scientists a starting point for tracking whether the problem increases or decreases over time.
Our findings highlight that even sacred springs thought to be pristine contained microplastics. This could harm aquatic life, diminish the waters' spiritual value and expose people who drink, collect or bathe in them. This shows the urgent need for broader water-quality monitoring of sacred springs across South Africa.
How plastic particles polluted the heart of sacred water sources
We investigated the sulfur-rich springs at Isinuka, near Port St. Johns, Eastern Cape, and freshwater systems at sites in Mbizana, Eastern Cape, and Bongwana, KwaZulu-Natal, where naturally occurring carbon dioxide (CO₂) enters the water. In simple terms, CO₂ naturally escapes from underground through cracks and fractures in the rocks, mixing with groundwater before it reaches the surface.
The Bongwana springs lie along a major crack in Earth called the Bongwana Fault, which allows gas and groundwater from deep underground to rise to the surface. This makes the springs rare and scientifically important.
Sacred springs may seem protected because many are in rural or undeveloped areas. But they are still affected by what happens around them. Plastic waste left on land can break into tiny pieces and be washed into the water when it rains. Plastic fibers can also travel through the air and fall into springs. Bottles and packaging used near the water may add more pollution.
The highest concentration was recorded at Isinuka Spring (also known as Isinuka Healing Spa or the naturally pink spring). Almost 70% of the transparent particles were fibers or filaments, likely from clothing and other textiles.
Hundreds of people visit Isinuka on a typical weekend. People have traveled there for generations for spiritual and physical healing, cleansing practices, water collection, tourism and small-scale commercial activities, including selling the water and mud to those who visit.
We do not know whether these activities caused the pollution because we could not trace where each piece of microplastic came from. But the large number of visitors and the presence of microplastics show why we need to investigate how microplastics are getting into heavily used sacred waters.
The other springs we visited in Mbizana and around Bongwana were generally smaller and used mainly by local communities. People visit them to collect water, carry out traditional and cultural practices, and experience the unusual bubbling produced by naturally occurring carbon dioxide.
Compared with Isinuka, we observed relatively little visible plastic waste around these sites, although microplastics were still detected in the water.
What communities think about the health and pollution risks
At the springs, we spoke with local community members about their experiences, beliefs and practices associated with the water. We also asked for their views on health and plastic pollution.
At Isinuka, people were collecting water and mud to sell and using the area for spiritual and traditional practices.
One of the vendors who sells spring water and mud at the site told us:
"I have used Isinuka's pinkish water and mud for years and have never experienced any related health problems."
The presence of microplastics does not mean that using the water will necessarily cause illness. However, where people drink, collect or bathe in spring water, it is important to understand how much exposure may occur and whether there are any associated health risks.
For some community members, the value of the Isinuka springs extends far beyond the physical properties of the water. One person explained:
"People come here because they believe in the healing power of the water. This place is important to our community and our traditions."
Another community member emphasized the responsibility to protect the site:
"We need to look after the spring because it is something we have inherited from our ancestors and should leave for the next generation."
When we asked community members why there was so little plastic litter around the carbon dioxide springs in Mbizana, one community member explained that people are encouraged to keep the springs clean:
"Plastic pollution is not really a problem here because we are encouraged to clean the springs after using them and to avoid littering. We always clean up when we visit, although sometimes other community members and visitors still leave trash behind."
Another community member said, "When people come here, they should respect the spring and take their trash with them when they leave."
This shows that communities already play an important role in caring for these sites. They also highlighted an important point: A spring can look clean while still containing microplastics that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
What needs to happen next
Our findings provide baseline evidence that microplastic pollution has reached sacred freshwater systems. Our next step is to determine where the particles come from, how their presence changes between seasons and whether they accumulate in sediments or aquatic organisms.
Protecting these springs means keeping them physically clean while preserving their ecological condition and cultural integrity. Scientists and government authorities can monitor pollution and investigate its sources.
Communities should be partners, bringing local knowledge and long-term observations together with scientific evidence. Communities and visitors can also reduce single-use plastics, take waste home and join cleanups.
Scientific evidence and community stewardship are both needed to keep these waters healthy and culturally meaningful for future generations.

title: Cães-selvagens vivem 'odisseia' percorrem 4 mil km e quebram recorde entre mamíferos africanos
content:
Cães-selvagens-africanos: espécie ameaçada é conhecida pela resistência e capacidade de percorrer grandes distâncias (Pexels)
Redatora
Publicado em 19 de setembro de 2026 às 06h35.
Três cães-selvagens-africanos percorreram 4.126 quilômetros pela Zâmbia, estabelecendo a maior rota de dispersão já registrada para um mamífero da África. A "odisseia", acompanhada por pesquisadores durante meses, revelou a capacidade desses animais de atravessar grandes áreas em busca de novos territórios e oportunidades de reprodução.
O deslocamento foi descrito em um estudo publicado na última quarta-feira, 9, na revista científica Ecology. Além do recorde, os resultados indicam que populações de cães-selvagens separadas por centenas de quilômetros podem estar mais conectadas do que se imaginava.
Os animais pertenciam à matilha Mayukuyuku, no Parque Nacional de Kafue, na Zâmbia. Em julho de 2025, quatro fêmeas de 3 anos deixaram o grupo. Cerca de duas semanas depois, três machos da mesma idade também partiram.
Para acompanhar os deslocamentos, pesquisadores instalaram uma coleira de rastreamento por rádio em um integrante de cada grupo.
Apesar de Kafue oferecer grande quantidade de presas e extensas áreas protegidas, os cães seguiram para regiões cada vez mais distantes. Ao longo da jornada, passaram por áreas com menor proteção e chegaram aos arredores de cidades como Kabwe, Kitwe e Ndola.
Em setembro do ano passado, depois de ambos os grupos percorrerem mais de mil quilômetros desde o território original, machos e fêmeas chegaram a se reencontrar durante um único dia. Depois, voltaram a seguir caminhos diferentes.
Os três machos continuaram para o leste, atravessaram dois grandes reservatórios e finalmente se estabeleceram em uma região próxima à escarpa do Vale do Rift, cerca de 419 quilômetros em linha direta do local onde nasceram. Por causa do trajeto sinuoso, no entanto, eles percorreram 4.126 quilômetros até chegar ao novo território.
Segundo os pesquisadores, trata-se da maior distância de dispersão já registrada para qualquer mamífero africano. Como comparação, os gnus podem percorrer até cerca de 1.800 quilômetros durante a migração anual entre Quênia e Tanzânia.
Os cães-selvagens-africanos (Lycaon pictus) vivem em grupos familiares com uma estrutura social rígida. Normalmente, apenas um casal dominante se reproduz dentro de cada matilha.
Animais subordinados podem permanecer no grupo ajudando a cuidar dos filhotes ou partir em busca de parceiros e de um território onde tenham maior chance de reprodução.
Os sete animais acompanhados tinham 3 anos e poucas perspectivas de se reproduzir permanecendo na matilha Mayukuyuku, segundo os pesquisadores. A espécie também possui características físicas favoráveis a longos deslocamentos, incluindo pernas compridas e grande resistência.
A trajetória das quatro fêmeas teve um desfecho diferente. Em outubro de 2025, dados da coleira mostraram que uma delas começou a realizar movimentos repetidos de ida e volta. Os pesquisadores consideram provável que uma das fêmeas sem coleira tenha ficado presa em uma armadilha de arame usada para caça, enquanto as outras permaneceram próximas.
Dias depois, a própria coleira de rastreamento foi cortada, interrompendo o acompanhamento do grupo. Segundo os pesquisadores, essas armadilhas estão entre as principais ameaças atuais aos cães-selvagens-africanos.
Os animais em dispersão também enfrentam riscos naturais. Leões podem matar adultos e filhotes, hienas disputam suas presas e a travessia de rios pode colocá-los diante de crocodilos.
O percurso também trouxe novas informações sobre a distribuição da espécie. Em determinado momento, os machos passaram a poucos quilômetros de um grupo de fêmeas localizado no leste da Zâmbia, a mais de 500 quilômetros de Kafue.
Para os autores, esse tipo de deslocamento sugere que populações aparentemente isoladas podem manter conexões entre diferentes ecossistemas do leste e do sul da África.
Há também sinais de recolonização de áreas onde os cães-selvagens haviam desaparecido. O Parque Nacional de Kasungu, no Malawi, por exemplo, registrou recentemente a presença da espécie pela primeira vez em mais de uma década.
Ao mesmo tempo, as enormes distâncias percorridas mostram o grau de fragmentação dos habitats. Os pesquisadores destacam, por isso, a importância de preservar corredores ecológicos entre áreas protegidas, permitindo que os animais se desloquem entre diferentes populações.
O cão-selvagem-africano está entre os mamíferos mais ameaçados do continente, e a conservação da espécie depende não apenas de reservas isoladas, mas também da manutenção das áreas utilizadas durante esses longos deslocamentos.

title: Araceli y Mayte, trabajadoras sordas, ejemplo de inclusión laboral en centros especiales de empleo
content:
Araceli y Mayte, trabajadoras sordas, ejemplo de inclusión laboral en centros especiales de empleo
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La tasa de empleo de las personas sordas se sitúa alrededor del 60%, superior a la media de las personas con discapacidad pero varios puntos por debajo de la población general.
A los 21 años, Araceli Pratdesaba empezó a notar que algo iba mal: le costaba distinguir sonidos superpuestos y seguir conversaciones en ambientes ruidosos. El diagnóstico llegó poco después: pérdida de audición en ambos oídos por una afectación del nervio auditivo. Con él, un largo proceso de aceptación que ella resume hoy con una frase: “Antes pensaba: ‘Y encima soy sorda’. Ahora digo: ‘Sí, soy sorda, ¿y qué?”.
La historia de Mayte Barroso no es muy diferente. Comenzó a notar una pérdida auditiva hace unos 20 años, cuando trabajaba en un puesto de oficina tras haber sido monitora de ocio y tiempo libre. Hoy, con una pérdida auditiva del 89% y de carácter degenerativo -cuyo posible origen genético todavía investigan los especialistas- Mayte usa audífonos en su día a día en su centro especial de empleo con total normalidad.
En el caso de Araceli, durante una década evitó los audífonos, hasta que el deseo de ganar independencia la llevó a dar el paso. Hace año y medio se incorporó como administrativa a una oficina en Barcelona de Integra CEE, uno de los centros especiales de empleo asociados a CONACEE, donde decidió apostar también por un segundo audífono para afrontar con seguridad sus nuevas funciones. Hoy trabaja con autonomía, se coordina con distintos equipos y describe el cambio como “un renacer”. En lo que respecta a Mayte, a su hipoacusia se suma una discapacidad visual que, no obstante, no le impide trabajar en Madrid como técnica de apoyo de otros empleados con discapacidad, incluidas otras personas sordas.
Una discapacidad que pasa desapercibida
Coincidiendo con la Semana Internacional de las Personas Sordas que se celebra hasta el próximo 27 de septiembre, la Confederación Nacional de Centros Especiales de Empleo (CONACEE) quiere poner nombre y rostro a una realidad que sus centros viven cada día: personas con discapacidad auditiva que, gracias a tener un empleo, han encontrado un espacio de autonomía e independencia. "Los ejemplos de Araceli y Mayte reflejan cómo los centros especiales de empleo (CEE) pueden transformar una discapacidad que a menudo pasa desapercibida en una fuente de desarrollo profesional", aseguran desde la entidad.
En este sentido, CONACEE recuerda que la tasa de empleo de las personas con discapacidad en España se sitúa en el 28,9%, frente al 69,7% de la población general, según datos del Instituto Nacional de Estadística. En el caso de las personas con discapacidad auditiva, la inserción laboral es mayor, pero sigue siendo muy baja, pues alrededor de la mitad de las personas sordas no trabajan, y su tasa de empleo es del 60%. Una brecha que, señala la patronal, se agrava en el caso de discapacidades como la auditiva, que al no percibirse a simple vista tienden a generar barreras de acceso al empleo que pasan desapercibidas tanto para las empresas como para la sociedad.
La inclusión no consiste solo en dar una oportunidad, sino en generar entornos de trabajo donde las capacidades de cada persona puedan desarrollarse
“Cuando hablamos de discapacidad, solemos pensar en lo que se ve. Pero hay discapacidades, como la hipoacusia, que no se perciben a simple vista y que, precisamente por eso, generan barreras de acceso al empleo que pasan desapercibidas. Los CEE llevamos años demostrando que, con los apoyos adecuados, estas barreras se pueden derribar”, afirma Albert Campabadal Blanco, presidente de CONACEE.
“Los casos de Araceli y Mayte muestran que la inclusión no consiste solo en dar una oportunidad, sino en generar entornos de trabajo donde las capacidades de cada persona puedan desarrollarse plenamente, con independencia de las barreras de partida. Eso es lo que hacemos en los CEE cada día”, concluye Campabadal.

title: Itogon Mountain Village builds a home for love above the clouds
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Itogon Mountain Village in Benguet has transformed from a small family café into a popular mountain destination featuring cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel, all designed to showcase the stunning Cordillera landscape.
- The Bernabe family, who initially opened Café Stella, expanded their business in response to customer demand for private events, leading to the creation of additional facilities while preserving the natural environment.
- The venue emphasizes inclusivity and local culture, hosting various celebrations and working with local suppliers, while promoting environmental sustainability and heritage preservation in the rugged mountainous region.
ITOGON, Benguet – You notice the mountains before almost anything else.
They appear through the glass walls, between the pines beside the cabins, and behind the altar of a wooden chapel where nearly every direction opens to another ridge.
At Itogon Mountain Village, the view is not decoration. It is the point.
The three-hectare property in Barangay Loacan has grown from a small family café into a mountain destination with cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel designed around an almost 360-degree view of the Cordillera landscape.
On September 19, after weeks of habagat rain, the sun finally returned. The timing coincided with the property’s first wedding open house, Love Above the Clouds, but the experience made clear why people had begun coming here long before the flowers, gowns, and reception tables arrived.
The Bernabe family made a simple bet: that people would leave the city for the mountains, and that the mountains themselves were enough.
It started with coffee
Itogon Mountain Village did not begin with plans for weddings. It began with Café Stella.
“We started off very small,” said lawyer Rish Bernabe, one of the family members behind the property.
There were about six employees and only around 15 items on the menu, she recalled. Their father had envisioned a café down the mountain, while the family, which had long spent holidays in Baguio and the surrounding highlands, took on the challenge of running it.
Opening outside Baguio was a gamble. The place is almost half an hour away from the city, so “building up a business here was really a risk,” Rish said. Then people came.
The café gained attention on social media, and a kitchen designed for a modest number of customers suddenly had to feed far more. So they expanded the kitchen, upgraded to commercial equipment, hired more workers, and opened more of the building.
From a handful of employees, the enterprise eventually grew to around 80, according to the family.
Customers then began asking to reserve the café for private events. Closing the restaurant for an entire celebration was difficult, so the family expanded again.
Cabins followed. Then the Chapel of the Mountains. Then Montesierra, a dedicated events space.
What started as somewhere to eat had become somewhere people wanted to stay, gather, and mark important days.
Building around the mountain
The growth could easily have changed what drew people there. But the Bernabes say they tried not to let that happen.
Glass dominates much of the architecture so that the surrounding mountains remain visible. Buildings and roads were adjusted around existing trees whenever possible, they said.
One tree remains standing in the middle of a road because the family refused to cut it.
“This is the yamang lupa that made us come here,” Rish said. “So we really have to preserve it and celebrate it.”
That approach is most evident at the Chapel of the Mountains.
Wooden pews face an altar framed by glass, pines, and distant slopes. Light falls through the roof. Turn to either side, and the landscape remains part of the room.
On that sunny September afternoon, after a long stretch of rain, no manufactured backdrop could really compete.
The chapel is also deliberately non-sectarian. It is not accredited by the Roman Catholic Church to host Catholic sacramental weddings, management clarified after earlier confusion over a ceremony held there.
Rish said the couple involved had already been legally married in Manila and that the ceremony at the chapel was symbolic.
“We respect the rules of the diocese,” she said.
The space remains open to other ceremonies consistent with legal and religious requirements.
Its openness, then, is not only architectural. It gives couples and families from different traditions a place to celebrate in their own way.
Love beyond weddings
That idea of inclusion was central to the September 19 gathering.
“Today is about love, and not just romantic love,” said Suzy Mejia Bernabe, who handles marketing and sales for the family enterprise.
She spoke about weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, reunions, and other milestones, but also about creating a place where people could “slow down and reconnect.”
The family says it works with local suppliers, uses local produce when possible, and invites local makers, artists, and cultural performers to take part in events. That puts the property within a broader effort by Itogon to build tourism around its landscape and culture.
The municipality has long been associated with gold. Its own historical account traces gold working in the area to Indigenous communities before the colonial period, while large-scale mining later shaped much of the town’s modern history.
Today, Itogon’s tourism program also promotes nature and culture, with environmental sustainability, heritage preservation, and local employment among its stated goals.
The setting comes with limits. Itogon is rugged mountain country, with 74.6% of its land classified as having slopes steeper than 50%, according to the municipal government.
The Bernabes know building here is different from building on flatter ground. The terrain dictates what can be done, where structures can go, and sometimes which trees have to stay exactly where they are.
Perhaps that is why the place works. It does not feel as though the mountain was flattened to make room for a destination. In places, the destination appears to have negotiated with the mountain.
Looking up
For generations, Itogon has been known for what lies beneath its mountains: gold.
Itogon Mountain Village asks visitors to look up instead. At the pines growing beside the buildings. At the ridges beyond the glass. At a chapel where mountains remain visible behind the altar.
The family started with a small café and the uncertainty that anyone would drive this far from the city. But now, people come not only for coffee, but to stay, celebrate, marry, or simply spend a few hours where the mountains are allowed to remain the biggest thing in the room.
Perhaps the distance is not something visitors have to overcome after all. Perhaps it is part of the point. – Rappler.com

title: Chesapeake Bay Blue Crab Numbers See Encouraging Bounceback in New Survey
content:
Conservationists working to turn the tide on declining numbers of blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay, found some good news in their latest field surveys.
After years of worryingly low numbers, the population appears to be responding to some of the measures implemented to build a crustacean comeback.
This year’s field sampling estimated a total population of 349 million blue crabs in the bay—a 46% increase over last year, according to the annual winter dredge survey.
This raised the population overall to the highest it’s been since 2019, says the report from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and Virginia Institute of Marine Sciences.
The population of juvenile crabs in winter 2025–26 was estimated to be 228 million, which is also the highest since 2019.
The largest estuary in the US, spanning 200 miles from Maryland to Virginia near Washington DC, the Chesapeake supports more than 3,600 plant and animal species—and the crab remains a cornerstone of the region’s heritage and culture.
In the past 30 years, the surface water temperature of the Chesapeake Bay has increased 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit, but our climate craziness—colder in the winter (which crabs don’t like) and hotter in the summer—isn’t the only cause of the crab conundrum. Human industrialization also plays a role.
MORE GOOD NEWS FROM THE BAY:
• Locally Extinct for a Century, Bay Scallops Thriving Again in Virginia’s Chesapeake
• World’s Largest Oyster Restoration Is Big Success – Fulfilling Virginia’s Promise to Chesapeake Bay Rivers
Also a problem, invasive ‘blue catfish’ are hunting and digging up dormant blue crabs year-round, after having been (stupidly) introduced in the 70s for recreational fishing.
Although recreational and commercial fishing was once a major contributor to falling numbers of blue crabs, the catch limit laws from Maryland and Virginia had solved that issue: separate research from the 2026 Chesapeake Bay Blue Crab Assessment and Advisory report showed no overfishing in the bay.
The numbers can go up and down abruptly, due to many factors, but the neighboring states and federal agencies continue to share data and commit resources to ensure a healthy ecosystem.
And their efforts are paying off. Maryland just released a new report confirming the abundance of underwater sea grasses in the Bay and its tidal tributaries in Maryland last year.
A BAY BEAUTY: Scientists Work to Turn the Tide of Oyster and Seagrass Decline in Chesapeake Bay, Often by Hand
Seagrass coverage—critical for the Bay’s health—expanded from 36,799 acres in 2024 to 41,419 acres in 2025, an increase of nearly 13% in a single year. Bay-wide, acreage reached an estimated 89,385 acres – up 7% from 83,252 acres in 2024.

title: National Park Service director calls Yellowstone's wild bison recovery an 'incredible conservation story'
content:
A little more than a century ago, Yellowstone's bison were hanging on by a thread.
Today, thousands of them roam the park. And the conservation challenge has shifted from simply saving the herd to figuring out how to manage a thriving one.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS
During an interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, called the recovery an "incredible conservation story."
After millions of bison once roamed the Great Plains, the animals were nearly wiped out across their historic range. Rebuilding those populations, Bowron said, has taken decades of careful scientific work and cooperation among the Park Service and its Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
"To show up at Yellowstone today and have the experience as a visitor of seeing a wild bison in a functioning ecosystem, I don't know that we could have predicted that 100 years ago," Bowron said.
That's a pretty remarkable turnaround.
And now, Yellowstone's bison are helping build conservation herds far beyond the park itself.
Yellowstone bison are finding new homes
Through the Bison Conservation Transfer Program, Yellowstone works with Tribal partners to relocate live bison that have completed the necessary quarantine process.
Since 2019, more than 600 bison have been transferred to 29 tribes across 13 states, according to Bowron. More than 200 were transferred in 2026 alone.
"This is one of the coolest parts of this entire conservation effort," Bowron said.
Once the animals are transferred, she explained, each tribe can manage its herd according to its own priorities and sovereignty.
"It's a great example of how we're able to establish and expand conservation herds through that kind of partnership," Bowron said.
But conservation success doesn't mean the work is finished.
In some places, rebuilding the population remains the goal. At Yellowstone, Bowron said the challenge now is largely about managing the healthy herd that's already there.
"I think at Yellowstone, we're in the latter — figuring out how to successfully manage the herd that we have with all of our partners," she said.
At the same time, the Park Service continues to pursue live-transfer opportunities with tribes interested in establishing or expanding conservation herds.
A conservation problem you want to have
The Yellowstone story is also a reminder that conservation wins don't happen overnight.
Bowron said rebuilding bison populations has taken decades of scientific monitoring and cooperation among Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
WHY TED TURNER'S APPROACH TO CONSERVATION IS THE MINDSET AMERICA DESPERATELY NEEDS RIGHT NOW
And even after a species rebounds, the work changes rather than disappears.
For generations, the question was whether wild bison could survive at all in places like Yellowstone.
Now, wildlife managers are dealing with a very different question: What do you do when the comeback works?
Bison don't care where Yellowstone's boundary lines are drawn. They move across a massive landscape, meaning managing a successful herd requires cooperation among the Park Service and the many communities and agencies surrounding it.
But the fact that there is a healthy herd to manage — and enough animals to help establish conservation herds elsewhere — would have been difficult to imagine a century ago.
For anyone who's ever sat in Yellowstone traffic because a bison decided the middle of the road belonged to him, it might be easy to forget just how close America came to losing that experience entirely.
SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER
Today, seeing those animals wander through the park feels almost inevitable.
It wasn't always.
So yeah, you can definitely call it a comeback.

title: In 2025, the ozone hole shrunk to one of its smallest sizes in decades
content:
The Antarctic ozone hole in 2025 was one of the smallest in decades—a testament to the continuing success of international action to protect Earth's ozone layer, which shields us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
In welcome news, the WMO Ozone Bulletin said that last year's ozone hole ranked as the fourth or fifth smallest since severe depletion patterns were observed in 1992. This is the second consecutive year that both the depth and extent of the ozone hole were significantly below the 1990–2010 average.
Year-to-year fluctuations are influenced by large-scale meteorological transport conditions, which drive springtime ozone depletion almost every austral winter above Antarctica and every five to 10 years in the Northern Hemisphere.
In the Northern Hemisphere, total column ozone in 2025 was below average (negative anomalies) in a large region extending from Greenland and Europe to Central Asia, northern Japan and the Kamchatka Peninsula in the Russian Federation.
These variations occur within the long-term trend toward the healing of the ozone layer, reflecting the success of the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, which phased out chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons once found in refrigeration, firefighting foam and other common uses.
"This is an environmental success story. Since 2000, the ozone layer has been recovering, and we can expect full recovery within several decades," said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo.
The WMO Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) network provides the critical, high-quality ground-based total column ozone observations required to accurately monitor ozone and ensure that long-term changes can be understood.
UV radiation
About 90% of atmospheric ozone resides in the upper stratosphere. If all this ozone were brought down to Earth's surface, the resulting layer of pure ozone would be only approximately 3 millimeters (0.12 inches) thick. Yet this thin layer blocks nearly all dangerous shortwave ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun and protects life on Earth.
While substantial progress has been made in addressing ozone depletion, measurements over the past decades show a significant increase in the number of days with high UV index values. The UV index was developed to track the depletion of the ozone layer and now serves as an international health standard for UV protection.
Since the mid-1990s, UV radiation has increased by as much as 20% in some parts of Europe. Ground-based measurements show that this has been driven primarily by a reduction in cloud cover and an accompanying increase in annual sunshine duration. Higher UV exposure means a greater risk of skin cancer and other UV-related diseases among exposed populations.
"In light of this trend, targeted and effective UV protection measures are of paramount importance," says the Bulletin.
World Ozone Day
The WMO Ozone Bulletin was released for World Ozone Day on Sept. 16, which celebrates the 1987 Montreal Protocol, which successfully phased out ozone-depleting substances. This year's theme is Global Action for a Cooler Planet, marking the 10th anniversary of the Kigali Amendment, which expanded the scope of the Montreal Protocol.
The 2016 Kigali Amendment provides for a phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), potent greenhouse gases used to replace ozone-depleting substances. These chemicals are widely used in everyday cooling technologies such as refrigerators, air conditioners, insulating foams and some medical and industrial equipment.
While they do not deplete the ozone layer, some HFCs trap thousands of times more heat than carbon dioxide, even though they remain in the atmosphere for a much shorter time.
Over the past four decades, atmospheric measurements have demonstrated significant reductions in the concentrations of controlled ozone-depleting substances. But there have been unexpected emissions, for instance of CFC-11 until 2018 and HFC-23. This is why atmospheric monitoring remains essential to support targeted regulatory actions by national authorities.
The Ozone Bulletin draws attention to the state of the observing system, which traditionally relied primarily on Dobson and Brewer spectrophotometers. The number of active stations has gradually decreased from around 130 in the early 2000s to 110 today—with stations often closing in areas where observations are sparsest.
Next-generation array spectrometers have grown rapidly, but these focus on air quality measurements rather than stratospheric ozone monitoring.
